opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think hardware is one of the most underappreciated constraints on what we can actually do in robot learning.

In language models, the "body" is basically fixed. You have text in and text out, and the frontier is set by data, compute, and architecture. In robotics, the embodiment determines what the model can even express. If your gripper is a simple parallel jaw, it doesn't matter how smart the policy is; you're not going to do dexterous in-hand manipulation. If your arm has limited payload or poor force sensing, you can't learn tasks that depend on feeling contact. So hardware sets a ceiling on capabilities before learning even enters the picture.

Hardware also shapes the data. Most of the progress we've seen recently comes from scaling up demonstration data and training large policies on it. How you collect that data depends heavily on the hardware: how easy it is to teleoperate, how reliable the robot is over thousands of hours, how cheap it is to deploy many units in parallel. A robot that breaks down every few hours or costs hundreds of thousands of dollars limits how much data you can gather, and data is the fuel. Cheaper, more robust platforms have driven a lot of the recent momentum because more people can collect more data in more diverse settings.

Hardware diversity matters too. Every lab has a different arm, gripper, and camera setup, which fragments the data. Cross-embodiment learning, training one model across many robot types, is an attempt to turn that fragmentation into an advantage, but it's still hard. The action spaces differ, the dynamics differ, and transfer isn't free.

Then there's the gap between what models can plan and what bodies can execute. Vision-language models now give robots strong semantic understanding. They know what a sponge is and what "clean up the table" means. But the bottleneck is often the low-level physical skill: precise, fast, robust manipulation with contact. That's where hardware and control matter most. Better actuators, better tactile sensing, and more compliant, safer designs let us push into tasks that were off-limits before.

So I see a co-evolution. Learning methods are getting much better at absorbing data and generalizing, but how far they reach in the real world depends on bodies that are capable, reliable, and affordable enough to deploy at scale. When hardware improves, it unlocks both new skills and new data, and that compounding effect is what will move the frontier.

r001.rationale: The candidate says embodiment determines what a model can express and that hardware sets a ceiling on capabilities before learning begins.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that for a long time in robotics we blamed the hardware, and I think that was mostly an excuse. If you look at what a Franka arm or a WidowX or even a Stretch can physically do when a human teleoperates it, the gap between that and what our policies could do autonomously was enormous. The hardware was clearly capable of folding the shirt or loading the dishwasher. The bottleneck was intelligence, and specifically it was data and the models that could absorb that data.

So for the last few years I'd argue hardware has not been what sets the frontier. Software has. The exciting thing about the RT-1, RT-2 era and then the Open X-Embodiment work was precisely that you could take fairly ordinary hardware, pool data across labs with totally different arms and grippers and camera setups, and get positive transfer. That told us the frontier was a learning problem, not a motor-and-actuator problem.

That said, I don't think that stays true forever, and I think we're starting to see the crossover. Once your policies get good enough that they're actually trying to do the hard things, the hardware starts to bite in a few specific ways. One is sensing: most robots have far worse tactile and force feedback than a human hand, and there are whole categories of manipulation, anything with deformables, anything in-hand, where you basically can't learn the skill if the signal isn't there. Two is reliability and cost: if you want to collect millions of episodes or deploy at scale, a robot that breaks every two hundred hours or costs a quarter million dollars caps your data flywheel in a way no model improvement fixes. And three is degrees of freedom. A parallel-jaw gripper can do a surprising amount, but there's a ceiling, and dexterous hands are where the hardware is genuinely immature.

So my honest framing is that hardware sets the ceiling and software determines how close you get to it. For most of the last decade we were nowhere near the ceiling, so hardware didn't matter much at the margin. Now the models are good enough that the ceiling is in view, and the most interesting question becomes a co-design question: what hardware do you build when you know the policy is going to be a large pretrained model that learns from demonstration rather than a hand-engineered controller? That changes what you optimize for. You care less about repeatability to the tenth of a millimeter and more about cheap, safe, robust, lots of sensors, and easy for a human to teleoperate so you can get data out of it. I think the labs and companies that treat hardware as a data collection instrument first, and a deployment platform second, are going to move the frontier fastest.

r001.rationale: The candidate explicitly says that “hardware sets the ceiling” on what AI can achieve, while software determines how close it gets to that ceiling.

astra-6.text:
I think robot hardware defines the interface through which intelligence can interact with the physical world. Your sensors determine what you can observe, your actuators determine what you can do, and the reliability of the system determines how much experience you can collect. So hardware is very much part of what sets the frontier.

But I’d distinguish between a hardware limitation and a learning limitation. If a robot can’t physically reach an object or exert enough force to lift it, a better model won’t solve that. If the hardware is capable of the motion but the robot can’t reliably figure out when and how to execute it, that’s a problem where better learning could make a huge difference.

The other piece is scale. A very sophisticated robot that requires constant maintenance can be less useful for advancing learning than a simpler robot that runs reliably all day. You need to collect experience, try things, fail, and improve. In that sense, hardware sets not just the frontier of what a robot could do, but also the pace at which we can learn to do it.

r001.rationale: The response says hardware helps set the capability frontier and explains that a model cannot overcome physical limits such as being unable to reach an object or exert enough force to lift it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think robot hardware sets a very concrete boundary on what intelligence can express in the physical world. You can have a very capable model, but if the robot can’t sense something, or its gripper can’t make the right contact, or its actuators can’t execute the motion reliably, then better reasoning alone won’t solve the task.

At the same time, I wouldn’t think of hardware as a fixed ceiling. Hardware and learning influence each other. The robot’s design determines what data you can collect and what behaviors you can explore. Then, as your models improve, you discover which limitations really require better hardware and which ones you can overcome through learning.

So the frontier is really in that interaction. You need hardware that’s reliable enough to collect experience at scale, and you need intelligence that can make effective use of the capabilities that hardware provides.

r001.rationale: The response says hardware sets a concrete boundary on what intelligence can express physically, giving sensing, gripper, and actuator limits as examples.
